# Iain McGilchrist — Resist the Machine Apocalypse (First Things, 2022)

## Bibliographic identity

Iain McGilchrist, "Resist the Machine Apocalypse," *First Things*, March 2022, published at firstthings.com. The issue month is recorded as March 2022 on the article's URL path and page furniture but must be verified against the print issue's masthead on acquisition; the record is marked accordingly. Wording below was captured from the web text this cycle; the final URL form and access date await a closing verification pass. This house exists because it is the citable, dated place where McGilchrist himself performs the AI mapping — the essay must not source that mapping to *The Matter With Things*, whose page-cites remain unverified (see Open acquisition).

## Source scholarship

This essay is McGilchrist's own explicit extension of the hemisphere thesis to artificial intelligence, and it matters to the source bank precisely because it is dated and quotable where the book-length treatments are not yet verified. Writing for a general readership, McGilchrist states the mapping directly: "AI… could in many ways be seen as replicating the functions of the left hemisphere at frightening speed." The claim is not that machines have hemispheres but that the machine's mode of operation — decontextualized token manipulation at scale — replicates the re-presentational modality his 2009 book assigned to the emissary. He supplies the mechanism in the same register: "The left hemisphere manipulates tokens or symbols for aspects of experience," which is the sentence that lets the essay align his account with symbol-processing descriptions of computation without stretching his words.

The essay's second movement is the reciprocal-assimilation claim: "As machines — or so it is claimed — become more like humans, humans are certainly becoming more like machines." The interpolated concession ("or so it is claimed") does real work and must be preserved in quotation: McGilchrist is skeptical of the machines-becoming-human half and confident only of the human drift toward machine-likeness. Together the three passages give the essay the citable, dated form of the AI-as-runaway-emissary claim — the emissary's mode of attention externalized, accelerated, and feeding back into its makers. For the source bank's discipline this house is a stand-in with a fence around it: *The Matter With Things* (2021) doubtless carries fuller versions, but its page-cites are unverified and it must not be cited until acquired; until then, every AI-mapping use routes through this article.

### Claim boundary

This is an essayistic claim by the author in a magazine of religion and public life, not peer-reviewed neuroscience; the essay uses it as a contemporary witness only. It inherits the full criticism gate of [[symbolon/episteme/sources/psychology/mcgilchrist/mcgilchrist-2009-master-emissary/mcgilchrist-2009-master-emissary.md|mcgilchrist-2009-master-emissary]] (the hemispheric framework it extends is contested), and nothing here licenses claims about how AI systems actually work.
